extracted.intended_audience: administrative-law scholars, federal judges, agency lawyers, and law students interested in APA rulemaking and interim-final rules
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the legality and reasonableness of interim-final rules (IFRs) and related final-final rules (FFRs) under the Administrative Procedure Act, focusing on § 553 notice-and-comment, the good cause exception, arbitrary-and-capricious review, and appropriate judicial remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with § 553 prepromulgation notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The familiar procedure of notice-and-comment rulemaking, set forth in § 553 of the APA, requires that agencies publish a general notice of a proposed rulemaking in the Federal Register, give 'interested persons an opportunity to participate in the rule making' by submitting comments, and then, '[a]fter consideration of the relevant matter presented,' issue a final rule along with a 'concise general statement of [its] basis and purpose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepromulgation notice and comment embodies Fullerian values (publicity, clarity, prospectivity). Benefits include public scrutiny, the ability to adjust the rule’s reach after receiving precise information, and producing a reasoned final explanation. Courts have grafted additional requirements (e.g., disclosure of studies, meaningful consideration of significant comments, logical outgrowth). Failure to adhere can give rise to procedural invalidity unless harmless error is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good cause exception (§ 553(b)(3)(B))
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA contains a 'good cause' exception that permits agencies to forego notice and comment if the procedure would be 'impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative-history meanings: 'impracticable' = agency functions would be unavoidably prevented by public rulemaking; 'unnecessary' = minor/technical amendments; 'public interest' supplements the others and applies where procedure would prevent agency operation or where lack of public interest warrants dispensing with procedure. Courts vary in applying the prongs; recommended reforms include demanding a link between an agency's factual reasons and the specific prong invoked and treating good-cause findings under de novo review to deter opportunistic invocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing in the Federal Register (§ 553(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive rules are subject to the APA’s requirement of publication in the Federal Register thirty days before going into effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication timing provides a modicum of notice to the public but does not substitute for the informational and deliberative benefits of prepromulgation comments. The thirty-day publication requirement mitigates—but does not eliminate—publicity concerns raised by IFRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmless error doctrine in APA judicial review (5 U.S.C. § 706)
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA’s judicial review provisions include a harmless error rule: a procedural omission that has been cured by affording the party the procedure to which it was originally entitled is not reversible error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may treat postpromulgation notice-and-comment as curing procedural defects where there is no prejudice. Harmless-error analysis allows courts flexibility (including remand without vacatur) and underpins some rationales for treating IFRs/FFRs as procedurally adequate in particular cases. However, reliance on harmless error can incentivize agencies to skip prepromulgation comment if courts routinely deem defects harmless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-mind (postpromulgation) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An intermediate circuit approach requiring that agencies keep an 'open mind' during the postpromulgation notice-and-comment period; courts would uphold IFRs subjected to postpromulgation comment only if the agency’s final rule reflected genuine consideration of comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several circuits adopted this standard to prevent agencies from using IFRs as foregone conclusions. The Supreme Court in Little Sisters rejected the open-mind test as a court-created procedural requirement not grounded in the APA’s text, thereby weakening this check. The open-mind test is discussed as a judicially fashioned protection tied to the harmless-error principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary-and-capricious substantive review (rational connection/fit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under § 706 and Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm, courts must ask whether the agency articulated a 'rational connection between the facts found and the choice made'—including whether the scope ('fit') of the rule accords with the problem the agency set out to address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'substantive' approach is the primary recommended tool to police IFRs and FFRs: assess overbreadth, failure to consider reasonable alternatives, and whether the agency accounted for important aspects (e.g., differentiated impacts across regulated entities). Examples: Justice Kagan’s concurrence in Little Sisters and the Texas v. Becerra district court’s overbreadth analysis. Advantages include addressing both IFRs and FFRs and accommodating harmless-error and flexible remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fullerian rule-of-law principles as evaluative standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Fuller’s eight principles: laws must be (1) generally applicable, (2) sufficiently publicized, (3) prospective in effect, (4) clearly understandable, (5) consistent with each other, (6) reasonable in what they ask of the populace, (7) relatively stable and unchanging, and (8) congruent with enforcement practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The APA’s notice-and-comment procedure embodies these values—publicity, clarity, prospectivity, reasoned justification, and stability. IFRs risk violating clarity, generality, and publicity: opportunistic IFRs can make rules appear ad hoc, obscure internal deliberation, and reduce perceived legitimacy. Courts mindful of Fullerian morality may scrutinize IFRs more strictly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies: remand without vacatur vs vacatur
rubrics_metrics.description: When a rule is procedurally or substantively deficient, courts can choose remedies including vacatur or remand without vacatur (retaining the rule in force while requiring further agency action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remand without vacatur is a targeted remedy that avoids disruption when an IFR has already changed regulated parties’ behavior; it has been used in EPA cases and is a flexible tool for courts concerned with practical effects. The choice of remedy should account for prejudice, the scope of the agency error, and public interest in regulatory continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural approach: policing IFRs through stringent good-cause review
rubrics_metrics.description: A procedural route to cabin IFRs would impose de novo review on agencies’ invocations of good cause and demand a clear link between the agency’s factual reasons and the specific prong of the good-cause exception it invokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach aims to create consistent standards for good-cause findings and deter opportunistic exemptions from § 553. Example: Association of Community Cancer Centers v. Azar, where the district court rejected a 'public interest' claim for a non-emergency financial-regulatory IFR. Downsides: risk of overly narrowing the exception and impairing agencies’ ability to respond to genuine emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of a reasoned explanation and meaningful consideration of comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rules must be accompanied by a 'concise general statement of their basis and purpose' and agencies must consider the 'relevant matter presented' in comments; courts expect reasoned justifications tying decisions to the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although § 553’s text is minimal, arbitrariness review and paper-hearing doctrines effectively require more elaborate justifications (disclosure of studies relied on, meaningful response to significant comments, showing logical outgrowth from proposed rule). Failing to connect factual findings to the rule’s scope or to explain why alternatives were rejected supports arbitrariness challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks from regulatory inertia and cognitive biases in postpromulgation processes
rubrics_metrics.description: IFRs and FFRs are vulnerable to 'regulatory inertia' and biases—status quo bias, confirmation bias, commitment bias—making agencies less likely to alter IFRs in response to postpromulgation comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because an IFR is already binding, postpromulgation comments are less likely to result in meaningful changes; inviting comments postpromulgation may be perceived as a pro forma exercise that undermines public trust and participation. Courts should factor in these tendencies when assessing whether postpromulgation comment cured procedural defects or whether substantive remediation is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit and scope analysis specifics (consideration of disparate impacts and alternatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should evaluate whether the agency applied evidence appropriate to all covered entities, considered differential impacts (e.g., on rural areas or staffing), and analyzed reasonable alternatives (e.g., testing instead of vaccination, exemptions for telework).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete fact patterns illustrate fit problems: applying data from long-term-care to psychiatric or community-care facilities; failing to assess staff shortages, rural healthcare impacts, or feasible alternatives. A thorough fit analysis supports arbitrariness findings where the rule extends beyond what the justification supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency/public-interest threshold for invoking good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'public interest' prong typically applies where delay would jeopardize 'life-saving importance' or the very reason for implementing the rule; general financial instability or cost savings are usually insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (e.g., Ass’n of Cmty. Cancer Centers) shows courts rejecting broad public-interest rationales when the asserted urgency is economic rather than immediate threat to life or core program functioning. Requiring a strict emergency threshold helps prevent routine circumvention of § 553.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper-record/full administrative record requirement to allow review
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have required the development of a full administrative record in informal proceedings so that they may evaluate whether an agency provided an 'adequate explanation' for its action (Overton Park, Vermont Yankee context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete record enables courts to test factual claims, assess the link between reasons and rule scope, and conduct meaningful arbitrary-and-capricious review. Failure to develop an adequate record hinders judicial review and supports remand or other remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on judicially adding procedural requirements (Vermont Yankee constraint vs interpretive latitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vermont Yankee bars courts from imposing additional procedural rights not grounded in the APA, but the opinion does not preclude courts from expansively interpreting the APA itself to require procedures with the effect of added protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tension guides judicial strategy: while courts should avoid inventing ad hoc procedures outside the APA, they can (and have) used substantive review and interpretive readings of the APA’s text to develop constraints on agency practice (e.g., requiring robust explanation, full records, or close scrutiny of good-cause claims).
